title.narrative: National child project under the GEF Africa Mini-grids Program Nigeria

description.narrative: Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.
Supporting access to clean energy by increasing the financial viability and promoting scaled-up commercial investment in minigrids in Nigeria.

The Nigeria child project will adopt a private sector minigrid delivery model, which, together with innovative business models centred on cost reduction levers, will catalyse private sector investments in solar PV-battery minigrids sustainability across multiple facets described in paragraph 56. Figure 3 has shown the qualitatively the causal relationships between multi-tier electricity access and local socioeconomic development that itself becomes a market pull for renewable electricity. The virtuous circle positively enhances the affordability of renewable electricity. GEF investments have been estimated to support directly 11,875 households (i.e. 70,063 persons of which 34,559 female), 600 connections for productive energy uses, and 375 connections to public infrastructure including schools and health clinics. Also, it has been estimated that around 1,263 direct formal jobs will be created in the construction, operation and maintenance of solar PV-battery minigrids, and in productive value chains considered using the load profile used in deriking analyses given in Annex 17 to the project document. Also, it is known that investments in solar PV minigrids also supports direct informal jobs, and these have been estimated at 583 jobs (Annex 18 to the project document). These socio-economic indicators are captured in the Results Framework (Annex A) for close monitoring during project implementation using the Monitoring Plan given in Annex 5 to the project document. The GEF financing will directly support the implementation of REA’s Rural Electrification Plan (Annex 13 to the project document). The analyses shown in Annex 17 to the project document reveal the full socio-economic impact of using a derisking approach to achieve REA’s plan of deploying 3.25 GW of solar PV by 2030. Although the GEF grant will contribute partially to the total derisking basket of policy and financial derisking instruments, it is worth summarizing the total derisking benefits towards which GEF funding is contributing. When implemented, the public derisking efforts lower financing costs and result in the following potential benefits: · serving approximately 75.35 million people (12.77 million households) to Tier 2-3 levels, including supporting productive energy uses (ligh engineering, commercial and agricultural activities) and electrifying social infrastructure (schools, primary health clinics and religious centres); · catalyzing USD 9,648 million in private sector investment in solar PV-battery mini-grids; · creating economic savings of USD 7,018 million over an investment lifetime of 20 years; · lowering average household daily energy spend via solar PV-battery mini-grid due to derisking from USD 37 cents to USD 28 cents; and · reducing emissions by 77.24 million tonnes of CO2 over 20 years, relative to the baseline.
